captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 11: Magnetism.
Maglev trains have no wheels:
powerful magnets lift them above the track and push them forward.
They use less energy than electric trains and emit far less carbon than diesel ones.
How else can magnets help us live more sustainably?
Every magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
Bring two magnets together: unlike poles attract, and like poles repel.
Materials attracted to magnets are magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt and steel.
Wood, plastic, glass, and even metals like copper and aluminium are non-magnetic.
Permanent magnets keep their magnetism, although heating,
hammering or dropping them can destroy it.
Temporary magnets, made of soft iron,
are magnetic only while in a magnetic field.
And electromagnets can be switched on and off.
A strong magnet is lowered over five objects: an iron nail,
a steel paper clip, a copper coin,
an aluminium can and a plastic spoon.
Predict: which objects will jump up to the magnet?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The magnet moves slowly down towards the objects.
Only the iron nail and the steel paper clip jump up.
The copper coin, the aluminium can and the plastic spoon stay on the table.
Explain what you saw.
Only magnetic materials are attracted: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
Copper and aluminium are metals, but they are not magnetic,
and plastic is not a metal at all.
So 'all metals are magnetic' is a common mistake.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Around every magnet is an invisible region where its force acts:
the magnetic field. Sprinkle iron filings around a bar magnet,
and they line up along the field lines.
The lines go from the North pole to the South pole,
and they're closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest.
The field gets weaker further from the magnet.
Move a magnet towards a paper clip,
and at a certain distance the force becomes strong enough to pull the clip across.
Magnetic force acts at a distance!
When two magnets come close, their fields interact.
Opposite poles: the field lines join up, and the magnets pull together.
Like poles: the field lines push apart, and the magnets repel.
Between them is a neutral point, where the forces cancel out.
Earth has a magnetic field too, shaped like a bar magnet's,
although there's no real magnet inside!
Moving molten metal in the outer core creates electric currents that produce the field.
Earth's field makes compass needles point north, helps birds navigate,
and protects us from fast charged particles from the Sun.
Its magnetic poles aren't quite at the geographic poles,
so maps show the difference.

Fields interact – and Earth is a magnet

captions: The Danish scientist Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass
needle moved whenever he switched on an electric current.
Electricity and magnetism interact!
Any wire carrying a current has a magnetic field around it.
Wind insulated wire into a coil around an iron nail,
and connect it to a cell and a switch.
Close the switch: current flows, the coil becomes a magnet,
the iron core is magnetised, and it picks up steel paper clips.
This is an electromagnet.
Open the switch: the current stops, the magnetism disappears, and the clips drop.
That's what makes electromagnets so useful: we can switch them on and off.
But don't leave the current on too long,
as the wire can get hot.
How can we make an electromagnet stronger?
First, add more turns to the coil.
Each turn adds to the overall magnetic field.
Second, increase the current flowing through the coil,
for example by adding more cells.
The bigger the current, the stronger the field.
Third, use an iron or steel core, which concentrates the magnetic field lines.
To test a factor fairly, change only one at a time: for example,
count the paper clips picked up with 10, 20 and 30 turns,
keeping the current and core the same.
A class makes an electromagnet with an iron nail,
using the same cell each time.
They count how many paper clips it picks up with different numbers of turns.
With 10 turns it picks up 3 clips.
With 20 turns it picks up 6, and with 30 turns, 9.
The points rise in an almost straight line: more turns, more paper clips.
Pause and decide: what is the independent variable,
and how many clips would you expect with 60 turns?
chapters: Real data: turns on the coil and paper clips picked up

captions: Electromagnets are everywhere. A loudspeaker has a coil behind its cone:
changing current makes a changing magnetic field that moves the cone, making sound.
Electric bells, motors in blenders and fans,
and computer hard drives all use electromagnets.
In industry, giant electromagnets on cranes lift scrap iron and steel,
then switch off to drop it.
Recycling plants use them to pull magnetic metals out of mixed waste.
Power station generators use spinning electromagnets to produce electricity.
In hospitals, MRI scanners use a huge magnet
to line up hydrogen atoms in your body.
Radio waves knock them out of line; as they flip back,
they release energy, which the scanner uses to build detailed pictures inside you.
Electromagnets are hidden inside many everyday things.
Here are four of them.
In an electric doorbell, pressing the button switches on an electromagnet.
It pulls a metal striker onto the bell, and the bell rings.
Some security doors are held shut by an electromagnet.
When a card is accepted,
the current is switched off and the door opens.
In speakers and headphones,
a changing current in a coil makes a changing magnetic field,
which moves a cone and makes sound.
At recycling centres, an electromagnet lifts steel cans out of mixed rubbish,
leaving the aluminium cans behind.
All of these work because an electromagnet can be switched on and off,
and its strength can be controlled.
Pause and think of one more device that might use one.

Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What happens when two North poles are brought together?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They repel.
Question 2: Name three magnetic materials.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Iron, nickel and cobalt (also steel).
Question 3: Give two ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
Pause the video now.
Answer: More turns, more current, or an iron core.
Question 4: Why are electromagnets used in scrapyards instead of permanent magnets?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They can be switched off to drop the metal.
